results.title: The B200 GPU Rental Price Illusion - Why Hourly Rates Lie About Who Pays What | AInvest
highlights:
The Nvidia NVDA-- B200 commands anywhere from $2.19 to $11.06 per GPU-hour in cloud rental pricing right now. That is the kind of spread that makes investors stare at a spreadsheet and conclude that the market is chaotic, the supply chain is breaking, or both. It is none of those things. The spread tells a much simpler story: who can get the chip, and who is being squeezed because they cannot.

...

The two-tier pricing reality

As of July 2026, B200 GPU rental on neo-clouds like CoreWeave CRWV--, Lambda, and Spheron starts between $2.69 and $5.50 per hour. The same GPU on hyperscaler platforms - AWS Capacity Blocks, for instance - runs near $9.36 per hour. That is more than a 2x premium for the identical hardware sitting in someone else's data center.

This is not a new phenomenon. It is the H100 playbook repeated with bigger numbers. When the H100 first arrived, hyperscaler pricing sat above $8 per GPU-hour while spot and neo-cloud rates eventually collapsed to $1.20-$3.50 per hour by mid-2026. The B200 is following the same trajectory, except the spread started wider because the chip is harder to come by.

What drives this gap? Supply allocation. Hyperscalers locked in B200 capacity through enterprise contracts and are now monetizing it at whatever the market bears. Neo-clouds, which operate on thinner margins and more aggressive utilization, pass savings through. For the end user, the question is not whether the B200 is expensive - it is whether you have a relationship that gets you the neo-cloud price.

...

Running the DeepSeek R1 model at 100 tokens-per-second per user, a B200 produces 497 tokens per second per GPU at $1.09 per million tokens. An H100 produces 23 tokens per second per GPU at $15.70 per million tokens.

...

Here is what the rental pricing spread obscures: the B200 is constrained. Data center GPU lead times sit at 36 to 52 weeks. Suppliers are issuing quotes with 24-to-48-hour validity windows - a signal that inventory positions shift so fast that pricing becomes meaningless before the customer can act.

results.title: Lambda GPU Cloud for Simulation: What You Rent and What It Costs | TechnoLynx
highlights:
Lambda GPU cloud rents NVIDIA GPUs as Linux virtual machines billed by the minute, from a single GPU up to reserved clusters of 16 to 512 H100 or B200 GPUs, with CUDA and the common frameworks already installed. Published on-demand rates for an H100 fall between roughly $3 and $4.30 per GPU-hour, depending on which source you read and when. Renting a fast instance does not make a simulation faster on its own. A serial physics loop leaves the rented GPU idle for most of each cycle, and Lambda bills every minute the instance runs, busy or not. For an RF propagation run, the speed-up comes from restructuring the algorithm. Our write-up on GPU-accelerating RF propagation simulation covers that redesign, and this page covers the rental side: what you get, what it costs and when it is worth paying for.

...

Lambda’s public cloud documentation describes two offerings. On-Demand Cloud launches individual GPU-backed virtual machines in 1x, 2x, 4x or 8x configurations, with B200, H100, A100 and GH200 among the GPUs offered. 1-Click Clusters are reserved clusters of 16 to 512 H100 or B200 SXM GPUs. They are connected by a 400 Gb/s InfiniBand non-blocking fabric in a rail-optimised topology and support GPUDirect RDMA at up to 3200 Gb/s.

...

## How is Lambda GPU cloud priced, and how should you compare its per-GPU-hour rates with hyperscaler GPU instances?

Lambda prices On-Demand instances per hour and bills them in one-minute increments. Billing starts when the instance passes health checks and stops when you terminate it. 1-Click Clusters are priced per GPU per hour but billed weekly under the terms of the reservation. Filesystems are billed separately, per GiB used per month. At the example rate in Lambda’s documentation of $0.20 per GiB per month, 1,000 GiB kept for a full month costs $200.

The published figures do not agree:

| Source | GPU | Rate per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lambda’s own instances page | H100 SXM | $3.99 |
| Lambda’s own instances page | B200 SXM6 | from $6.69 |
| Silicon Analysts tracker, 1x instance | H100 SXM | $4.29 |
| Silicon Analysts tracker, 8x instance | B200 | $6.99, limited availability |
| SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX guide, Lambda on-demand | H100 SXM | $2.99 |
| Silicon Analysts tracker, AWS Capacity Blocks | B200 | about $9.36 |

The same tracker also quotes Lambda’s B200 at about $5.50 and its on-demand H100 at $3.99 elsewhere on the page. Treat every number in that table as a dated snapshot, not as a price list.

The hyperscaler side changes too. AWS announced price cuts of up to 45% on its P4 and P5 GPU instances, and up to 44% on the H100-based P5 for On-Demand. For comparison, Lenovo’s 2025 TCO study used $98.32 per hour for an 8x H100 AWS p5.48xlarge, which is $98.32 ÷ 8 = $12.29 per GPU-hour. Whether that rate came before or after the cut is not stated. SemiAnalysis’s general reading is that hyperscalers charge more than neoclouds because they mainly serve enterprises.

To compare like with like, we would put four things side by side beyond the headline rate:

1. What the rate bundles. For most neoclouds the per-GPU price includes CPU, networking, power, local NVMe and a working Slurm and driver setup.
2. Consumption model. On-demand is the most flexible and usually the most expensive. Spot is cheaper but can be interrupted, and reserved contracts lock in a price.
3. Interconnect quality for multi-node jobs. Network fabrics with the same nominal speed perform differently in practice, and SemiAnalysis recommends validating them with nccl-tests.
4. Availability of the exact GPU. In early 2026, B200 capacity was constrained, and many providers offered it by reservation only.

results.title: AWS Just Raised GPU Prices 20%. Here Is What You Should Actually Be Paying for an H100 | ServerGurus
highlights:
By ServerGurus 11 July 2026 4 min read

AWS raised GPU instance prices again on July 1. That makes two hikes this year: 15% in January, another 20% in July. If you are renting GPU instances on AWS right now, you are paying roughly 35% more than you were on January 1 for the exact same hardware. And you were already overpaying back then.

Here is the math, why it is happening, and what independent GPU providers charge for the same NVIDIA silicon.

## The Numbers: AWS vs Independent GPU Providers

The latest AWS pricing, as of July 2026:

| GPU Instance | GPU | On-Demand / Hour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P5 (H100) | NVIDIA H100 80GB | $5.19 |
| P6-B300 (Blackwell) | NVIDIA B300 | $14.04 |
| G6 (L40S) | NVIDIA L40S 48GB | $2.24 |

Compare that to independent GPU cloud providers running the same hardware:

| GPU | Independent Price / Hour |
| --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 80GB | $2.01 |
| NVIDIA L40S 48GB | $1.25 |
| NVIDIA A100 80GB | $1.90 |

AWS is charging 2.5x to 3.5x more than independent providers for the same NVIDIA GPUs. On an H100, that is roughly $2,300 more per month, per GPU. If you run a four-GPU training cluster, AWS costs you an extra $9,200 every month compared to an independent provider.

...

First, NVIDIA cannot make enough GPUs. HBM3e memory is the bottleneck. Each stack costs $300, and an H200 needs four of them. NVIDIA cut RTX 50-series production by 30 to 40 percent because the memory is being redirected to data center GPUs. Supply is tight and getting tighter.

Second, AI demand is not cooling off. Enterprise AI spending hit $401 billion this year and keeps climbing. Every startup, every enterprise, and every government research lab wants GPUs. Demand is outstripping supply, and AWS is pricing accordingly.

The newest accelerators have moved from launch to broad availability quickly, with H200 and B200 already listed by hundreds of operators, yet the specialist neocloud segment remains light on network footprint compared with the established cloud and carrier operators that also sell GPU. For a buyer, the practical consequence is simple. The shortlist worth building is not the fifteen famous names, it is the far larger set of verified operators, where knowing which of them actually run the hardware is the difference between a real quote and a reseller markup.

results.title: AWS GPU Prices Jump 20% as Multi-Year Deals Replace Spot Market — TechReaderDaily
highlights:
On July 1, 2026, Amazon Web Services raised on-demand pricing for its GPU-backed EC2 Capacity Blocks by roughly 20 percent across the board. The new hourly rate for a single Nvidia accelerator inside a P6-B300 instance landed at $14.04. A P6-B200 now bills at $12.355 per accelerator-hour. Even the previous-generation P5, which runs Nvidia's H200 silicon, ticked up to $5.191 in US regions, Yahoo Finance reported on June 26. These are list prices. The actual availability of those instances at those list prices, on demand, without a prior reservation, is a separate question the public pricing page does not answer.

The price hike itself is not surprising. What is notable is that AWS published it at all. For most of 2025, the effective price of frontier GPU compute was discoverable only through a broker, a sales rep, or a three-year committed-use discount negotiated under non-disclosure. The fact that AWS has reset its public list prices upward signals that even the sticker price is now being pulled toward the market-clearing rate, a rate that the neocloud ecosystem has been setting in plain view for at least twelve months.

...

Campbell sketched the economics of a representative deal: a one-year reservation for 1,000 Nvidia B300 accelerators, priced at $5 per chip per hour. That single contract clocks in at roughly $45 million for twelve months. Even a channel partner taking a five percent margin walks away with a couple million dollars. The math Campbell offered was illustrative, not a specific client invoice, but the $5-per-B300-per-hour figure aligns with what several neocloud providers have been quoting to enterprise buyers since early 2026.

...

The spot market for frontier GPUs, the kind where a startup could spin up a hundred H100s for a weekend fine-tuning run with a credit card, has effectively ceased to exist. Allocation today happens through reservation contracts that run twelve to thirty-six months, often with non-refundable commitments attached. The neoclouds are filling a structural gap: enterprises that cannot get GPU instances from AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure at the scale they need, or cannot wait the six to nine months it takes for on-premise Nvidia deployments to be racked and cabled, are routing their budgets through CoreWeave, Crusoe, Lambda, Nebius, and Vultr instead.

...

The economics of training have therefore bifurcated the market: inference workloads can still find spot capacity on last-generation hardware, particularly A100 and H100 instances that are being displaced
